items.title: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% — cementing rate hike expectations
items.summary: U.K. inflation rose by a hotter-than-expected 3.5% in the 12 months to September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels.
items.body: U.K. inflation rose by a hotter-than-expected 3.5% in the 12 months to September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels. Economists polled by Reuters had been forecasting an annual inflation rate of 3.4%. September's print marked a continuation of the U.K.'s upward trend for inflation, which came in at 3.1% in August and 2.9% in July. The September reading was the highest annual inflation figure in almost a year. The U.K.'s Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday that the motor fuel inflation rate had hit its highest level since August 2022, when fuel costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Britain is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks, such as the U.S.-Iran war and the subsequent struggle to move oil through the Strait of Hormuz. U.K.

items.title: BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds
items.summary: Rick Rieder, BlackRock's CIO of global fixed income, lays out his expectations for the fourth quarter and where he sees the best opportunities.
items.body: Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview. Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration. "Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook , released Wednesday.

items.title: Faisal Islam: Inflation and borrowing figures illustrate chancellor's Budget challenge
items.summary: The economic figures released on Wednesday show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his Budget.
items.body: The chancellor was on an early flight to North East Scotland on Wednesday to announce new North Sea energy approvals as the last set of major economic figures dropped. From a mile high, as well as close up, the figures for inflation and for the public finances set out his Budget balancing act in clear terms. The National Debt has topped £3 trillion for the first time in the official figures. The headline rate of inflation has hit 3.5% and is surely heading back up to 4% in the coming months. Borrowing is running ahead of forecasts, as spending and interest costs increase. These show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his statement next week. On the one hand he says he wants to give "breathing space" to consumers yet again feeling the heat from cost of living pressures.

items.title: Double blow to Healey as inflation rises to 3.5% and monthly deficit hits £24bn
items.summary: Consumer prices rise by more than expected while government’s debt interest payments surge to record high for September Inflation surged to 3.5% last month while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn, in a double dose of bad news for John Healey before next…
items.body: Inflation surged to 3.5% last month while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn, in a double dose of bad news for John Healey before next week’s budget. The Office for National Statistics said annual inflation rose from 3.1% in August , overshooting City forecasts of a rise in the consumer prices index (CPI) to 3.4%, as a result of the surging cost of fuel. Oil and gas prices have soared since the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran , throttling the flow of fuel through the strait of Hormuz. Rising inflation has also contributed to higher government borrowing costs – the key factor behind the deterioration in the public finances since the spring statement in March.

items.title: US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors
items.summary: As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace maritime trade.
items.body: The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran , this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult. On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast. Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) . The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey.

items.summary: Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more…
items.body: Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the first part of this series, Frank Chen and Alice Li track the ways top-level policy decisions flow down to local officials – and the challenges those officials face in balancing a wide set of priorities. When many took time off to enjoy China’s National Day holiday earlier this month, stories from media outlets in the eastern province of Jiangsu showed the region’s Communist Party chief, Xin Changxing, hard at work. He started the day by conducting a safety inspection at a metro station, then visited local shops to see how sales were faring over the holiday.

items.title: How Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russia crippled the world’s second-largest diesel supplier
items.summary: President Donald Trump has blamed Ukraine for surging diesel prices that are hurting Republicans' election chances with the midterms just two weeks away.
items.body: Ukraine launched massive drone assaults against Russia this week, hitting key oil infrastructure and signaling Kyiv intends to block the Kremlin from increasing diesel exports in defiance of President Donald Trump . More than 1,000 Ukrainian drones targeted Russia on Sunday alone in one of the largest attacks this year, according to state media reports. The strikes set ablaze an oil export terminal in St. Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city and President Vladimir Putin 's hometown. Kyiv has ended its brief adherence to an energy ceasefire that Trump declared between Ukraine and Russia on Oct. 11. Moscow ignored that truce from the start and Kyiv vowed to retaliate.

items.title: Car buyers are demanding lower prices and better tech. Automakers must deliver both
items.summary: Bain says tech leads purchase considerations in China while price remains No. 1 in the U.S. and Europe, as pressure mounts on Western carmakers.
items.body: Global automakers face an increasingly demanding customer: one who wants both competitive prices and better technology, according to Bain & Company. Tech and features were a leading purchase consideration for 58% of Chinese consumers, ranking ahead of price, the consultancy's latest Global Automotive Consumer Survey found. In the U.S. and Europe, price remained the top consideration, cited by 68% and 62%, respectively. However, that does not mean Chinese buyers have stopped caring about affordability. Intense domestic competition has made low prices an expectation in China, pushing carmakers to stand out through technology and features, Bain executives told CNBC. Stricker expects Western markets to follow, with competitive pricing becoming a baseline and technology playing a bigger role in purchasing decisions.

items.title: Inflation and government borrowing highest for a year ahead of next week's Budget
items.summary: Inflation accelerated to 3.5% from 3.1% in the year to September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
items.body: UK inflation and government borrowing both hit their highest in a year on Wednesday, adding to the pressure on Chancellor John Healey ahead of his first Budget in a week. The pace of UK price rises accelerated to 3.5% in the year to September, pushed up by sharp increases in petrol and diesel prices. The inflation figures came as UK government borrowing jumped to nearly £25bn in September, which means borrowing for the financial year to date is running £6bn above official forecasts. Healey has promised a Budget which will keep to Labour's commitment not to hike the three main taxes - income tax, National Insurance and VAT - while sticking to the party's fiscal rules. Inflation, the rate at which prices are rising, jumped from 3.1% in the year to August to 3.5% in the year to September.

items.title: Flaw in PHP computer language leads to shutdown of websites around world
items.summary: Precautionary takedowns come as experts say bad actors could exploit vulnerability in language used by 70% of sites Websites around the globe have gone dark after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web. Belgian, Dutch,…
items.body: Websites around the globe have gone dark after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web. Belgian, Dutch, Finnish, French and German sites were among those that governments took down temporarily as they scrambled to patch the critical weakness in PHP, a language used by almost 70% of websites . The vulnerability in the programming language, which became public on Tuesday, sparked warnings from national security agencies in Washington and London. It means millions of websites will need to be fixed. One internet infrastructure expert said Russian state actors or organised criminals could exploit the flaw to carry out cyber-attacks. Wordpress, one of the most common website systems, uses PHP, as does Wikipedia, the messaging software Slack and – at least historically – much of Facebook.

items.title: Philip R. Lane: Euro liquidity lines and the international monetary system
items.body: Since the ECB only has domestic counterparties in its refinancing operations, it is essential to complement the domestic liquidity framework with international liquidity lines. These lines, which consist of both repo and swap lines, mitigate adverse spillovers in the event of increased demand for euro liquidity abroad and/or impairment in cross-border euro liquidity flows. In the absence of international liquidity provision, such shocks might exert upward pressure on euro money market rates or disrupt the functioning of securities markets and the banking system, and thereby impair monetary policy transmission. In recent years, the world economy has undergone profound structural shifts related to geopolitics and changes in the international financial system.

items.title: Tesla’s ‘flying car’ draws public concern in China – and an official response
items.summary: The Communist Party’s flagship newspaper has urged the public not to underestimate China’s technological achievements after Tesla’s “flying car” demonstration sparked concern in some quarters that the country may be falling behind in the global auto race. The People’s Daily…
items.body: The Communist Party’s flagship newspaper has urged the public not to underestimate China’s technological achievements after Tesla’s “flying car” demonstration sparked concern in some quarters that the country may be falling behind in the global auto race. The People’s Daily commentary, published on Wednesday, followed the American electric vehicle giant’s unveiling last week of a second-generation Roadster fitted with thrusters developed with SpaceX, the rocket company led by Tesla CEO Elon Musk. Footage showed the sports car climbing a curved ramp, flipping upside down in mid-air and landing on its wheels. Tesla said it planned to begin production in 2028. The showcase prompted online debate in China about the country’s position in the global auto race.

items.title: Tesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declines
items.summary: Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results.
items.body: Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue dropped. The stock was little changed in extended trading. Tesla's earnings report lands a day after CEO Elon Musk told investors on SpaceX's quarterly call that it would be a "good idea" for his two companies to merge, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up. "I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the call, responding to a question about a potential merger. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this." On the Tesla side, that means needing a 50% vote of all shares, which is "quite a high hurdle," he said. Musk addressed the matter in his opening comments on the Tesla call, but didn't provide any additional information.

items.title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
items.summary: The fine is the largest to date against Facebook's owner, larger than an $18bn deal with California.
items.body: Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices. A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data. "The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices". Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful. The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.

items.title: Stratford International on track to get cross-Channel trains in budget boost
items.summary: Sadiq Khan says upgrade would unlock station’s true potential and allow it to live up to its name Stratford International train station in east London will receive funding in next week’s budget, according to reports, putting it on track to live up to its name and become a hub…
items.body: Stratford International train station in east London will receive funding in next week’s budget, according to reports, putting it on track to live up to its name and become a hub for cross-Channel services. London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, has been making a case to ministers for funding to upgrade the station to allow it to start running international rail services. Until now only domestic routes running to and from central London and Kent have stopped at the station, although Eurostar services pass through on the way to and from St Pancras. Khan said: “We’ve been working closely with the government to make Stratford International truly ‘international’ for the first time – opening up new opportunities for jobs, investment and tourism, while connecting one of the UK’s fastest-growing economic centres directly to Europe.

items.title: China’s offshore tax crackdown could inadvertently fuel a digital dollar boom
items.summary: From October 22, China’s grace period for the disclosure and settlement of certain offshore-trust tax liabilities ends. For the Chinese government, this deadline highlights its desire to affirm control over capital outflows, while for Chinese high-net-worth families, it serves…
items.body: From October 22, China’s grace period for the disclosure and settlement of certain offshore-trust tax liabilities ends. For the Chinese government, this deadline highlights its desire to affirm control over capital outflows, while for Chinese high-net-worth families, it serves as a reminder that it is now harder to keep international assets beyond the reach of the government. The deadline sits against the backdrop of China tightening scrutiny around cryptocurrency, stablecoins and real-world asset tokenisation. The authorities have reaffirmed that all cryptocurrency-related activities remain illegal, while also imposing strict limits on yuan-pegged stablecoins both within and outside the country and on tokenised-asset activity outside approved financial infrastructure.

items.title: CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike and stock sinks
items.summary: CoreWeave shares are down 29% in October, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening.
items.body: CoreWeave is facing a crisis of confidence on Wall Street that's playing out in real time among equity and bond investors. With interest rates spiking and AI buildout concerns mounting, debt-heavy neoclouds like CoreWeave are being viewed by many market participants as the most vulnerable trade in the artificial intelligence space. "Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, a credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday, referring broadly to corporate debt in tech. Keches highlighted the "speed at which AI vibes are shifting on a day-to-day basis." CoreWeave, which went public in March of last year and reached a peak market cap of about $90 billion three months later, is now valued at roughly $34 billion, with its stock down 29% this month. Its unsecured debt, meanwhile, is sporting a yield of about 15%.

items.title: Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
items.summary: The prime minister provided little detail, and there are questions over shifting the fees onto unit costs.
items.body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills. These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used. Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill. But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock £27 off a typical annual bill. During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills".

items.title: Energy secretary leaning towards rejecting Rosebank oilfield
items.summary: Exclusive: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh minded not to give approval in victory for climate campaigners Miatta Fahnbulleh is minded to reject the giant Rosebank oilfield, sources have told the Guardian, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major…
items.body: Miatta Fahnbulleh is minded to reject the giant Rosebank oilfield, sources have told the Guardian, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners. After approving the smaller Jackdaw gasfield on Wednesday, officials say the energy secretary is leaning towards refusing approval for what would be one of the biggest oilfields in the North Sea. But she could still be overruled by Andy Burnham, who may hear different representations from the chancellor, John Healey. A final decision is expected before the end of this year.

items.title: The EU will ‘pull its punches’ on China despite growing trade war talk: analysts
items.summary: The European Union is likely to avoid a full-blown trade confrontation with China due to internal divisions in the bloc and fear of retaliation, according to a prominent research firm. The projection comes amid speculation that the two sides are on the brink of a trade war, with…
items.body: The European Union is likely to avoid a full-blown trade confrontation with China due to internal divisions in the bloc and fear of retaliation, according to a prominent research firm. The projection comes amid speculation that the two sides are on the brink of a trade war, with European policymakers raising the alarm about a looming “China shock 2.0” and pushing for stronger measures to protect domestic producers from Chinese competition. But the bloc would “continue to pull its punches” in any confrontation with Beijing due to a lack of consensus among and within Europe’s member states, the London-based Capital Economics said at an event in Hong Kong on Wednesday. The EU also had “concerns over retaliation” if it stepped up trade tensions with China, the research firm said, and held “lingering hopes to save the rules-based global trading system” that had helped Europe in the past.

items.title: Trump denies ordering Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, says he doesn't know who did
items.summary: Asked if Elon Musk ordered the slowdown, Trump said, "I don't know who did it, but I was not involved."
items.body: President Donald Trump on Wednesday insisted he had nothing to do with a slowdown of SpaceX 's Starlink in Ukraine and said he does not know if Elon Musk was responsible for speed-capping the critical satellite service. Trump's latest denial came one day after The Wall Street Journal , citing unnamed U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter, reported Musk ordered the slowdown and discussed it with Trump. "I wasn't involved," Trump told a reporter when asked about the decision as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in South Carolina. When pressed to answer if Musk, SpaceX's founder and CEO, ordered the slowdown, Trump said, "I don't know who did it, but I was not involved." The recent disruption of Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, rendered some Ukrainian drones effectively useless, weakening defenses against Russian attacks.

items.title: The tech helping crack decades-old cold cases
items.summary: Investigative genetic genealogy can help hunt down criminals but raises worries over privacy.
items.body: Randy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois. The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma. The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found. For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator. The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US. Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases.

items.title: Tesla beats earnings projections after Musk floats SpaceX merger plan
items.summary: Musk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of Tesla shareholders Investors will be paying close attention to Tesla’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday afternoon, after chief executive Elon Musk floated the idea of merging the…
items.body: Investors will be paying close attention to Tesla’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday afternoon, after chief executive Elon Musk floated the idea of merging the car company with his rocket and AI company, SpaceX. On a call with SpaceX investors on Tuesday, Musk said: “There’s a lot of merit to combining the companies.” Musk said that the board of directors for both of his businesses had put together special committees to explore the potential merger, but had not yet reached an agreement on the terms of the transaction. The move would require the approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders. Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings on Wednesday, with a reported revenue of $28.05bn and $0.48 on earnings per share. That beat Wall Street’s projections of $27.9bn in revenue, with $0.43 on earnings per share.

Wider use of the Chinese currency, also known as the renminbi, would support China’s high-quality growth while offering an alternative that could help stabilise the international financial system amid intensifying geopolitical risks, said Zhu Min, a former deputy governor of China’s central bank, in an article published in Communist Party press organ the People’s Daily on Wednesday.

items.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
items.summary: Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties related to Cambridge Analytica scandal in New Mexico.
items.body: Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.

items.title: Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
items.summary: Kashim Chowdhury was contracted for 183 hours a week, more than the number of hours in seven days.
items.body: The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent". Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood. He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021. The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain. The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs.

items.title: Booking.com under investigation by EU regulators over fake listings and scams
items.summary: European Commission calls accommodation website’s approach to fraudulent listings and phishing scams as ‘absolutely substandard’ EU regulators have opened an investigation into Booking.com, alleging that the accommodation website has not done enough to protect consumers from…
items.body: EU regulators have opened an investigation into Booking.com, alleging that the accommodation website has not done enough to protect consumers from fake listings and scams. The European Commission , which regulates the world’s biggest tech companies operating in the EU, said Booking.com may have breached the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) with its “absolutely substandard” approach to tackling fraudulent listings and phishing scams, where criminals impersonate a third party to trick people to hand over money. A commission official said Booking.com should be carrying out risk assessments and acting to prevent fraud as required under the DSA. “We feel that what they have done is absolutely substandard,” said the official.

items.summary: SpaceX shares jumped after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger.
items.body: SpaceX stock jumped 10% Wednesday after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a potential SpaceX- Tesla merger. The space company, which made its debut on the Nasdaq in the biggest initial public offering ever in June, reported third-quarter revenue on Tuesday of $14.6 billion, up 161% from the previous year, and beating LSEG consensus estimates of $12.72 billion. Meanwhile, its operating income came in at $2.8 billion, with net income of $4.4 billion, after reporting a net loss of $1.05 billion in the same period a year earlier. On an earnings call, Musk said he's considering a combination with Tesla — which would mark the largest merger in history — and that the boards of both companies have created specific committees to discuss a consolidation.

items.title: What is happening to UK prices?
items.summary: UK inflation rose in September, pushed up by higher petrol and diesel prices.
items.body: Inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in the year to September, the highest rate in nearly a year and above the Bank of England's 2% target. The rise was slightly higher than economists had predicted, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices. For example, if a bottle of milk costs £1 but is £1.05 a year later, then annual milk inflation is 5%. The prices of hundreds of everyday items, including food and fuel, are tracked by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). This virtual "basket of goods" is regularly updated to reflect shopping trends, with alcohol-free beer, dashboard cameras, and pet grooming equipment among items added in 2026 , while premium bottled lager and sheets of wrapping paper were removed. The ONS uses price changes in the basket of goods over the previous 12 months to calculate inflation.

items.title: French borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets
items.summary: Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook…
items.body: France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets. With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone. The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor ( Oat ) , issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%. The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasingly violent street protests in recent weeks.

items.title: Intel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that’s at least 5 years behind schedule
items.summary: Intel has installed the first major structural truss at its delayed Ohio chip fab, but the company has yet to announce a major outside customer.
items.body: Intel has hit a milestone in the construction of its massive chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio, that's running at least five years behind schedule, a delay that's coincided with soaring demand for advanced chips. On Wednesday, Intel announced that crews have installed the first major structural truss in Ohio, which means the next part of the construction has finally begun. "This represents another significant step toward expanded U.S. leading-edge semiconductor capacity," Intel Foundry head Naga Chandrasekaran wrote in a post on the company's website on Wednesday. In September, reports surfaced that the world's leading maker of high-bandwidth memory, SK Hynix , could team up with Intel in Ohio to lease some foundry space to make memory chips at the new site. Neither company would confirm any plans.

items.title: Giant tunnel proposed to tackle Windermere sewage discharges
items.summary: United Utilities, Environment Agency and local campaigners say 12-mile tunnel could take sewage away from England’s largest lake Plans are under way for a new giant tunnel to transport sewage away from Windermere, England’s largest lake. Windermere, in the Lake District, has…
items.body: Plans are under way for a new giant tunnel to transport sewage away from Windermere, England’s largest lake. Windermere, in the Lake District, has suffered from widespread raw sewage and bacterial pollution driven by discharges from United Utilities . Campaigners say this pollution has caused more frequent toxic blue-green algal blooms, with the public advised to avoid swimming in the lake. Modelling indicates the climate crisis will exacerbate these challenges, with the catchment expected to experience more intense rainfall over the coming years, placing further pressure on the wastewater infrastructure. A new project, backed by United Utilities, the Environment Agency and local campaigners, has set out a vision to end sewage discharges into the lake by building an 12-mile (19km) tunnel to transport sewage away from the lake.

items.body: Former Chinese central bank governor Zhou Xiaochuan has warned that failed artificial intelligence investments could trigger financial turbulence and urged preparations to mitigate risks amid concerns over a potential bust of the AI investment bubble. “Consider[ing]... such a large amount of the investment going to the AI facility; if a part of it goes to failure, it causes financial turbulence, and this may create a crisis,” Zhou said during a panel discussion at the Bund Summit in Shanghai on Tuesday. “It needs a very large action to bail out our economy [and] some of the financial institutions.” He called for more research and preparation, as well as tools to mitigate the potential fallout from failed AI investments. Zhou’s comments come amid concerns over excessive investment in AI-related sectors, with a sell-off in AI stocks on Wall Street last week.

items.title: What an eyesore! My day at Norfolk’s frightful fridge mountain
items.summary: This summer alone, 26 local authorities in the UK had to stop accepting fridges and freezers for recycling. Now the appliances are piling up around the country – with no proper disposal date in sight Not much is happening in the tiny Norfolk hamlet of Little Hautbois on the day…
items.body: N ot much is happening in the tiny Norfolk hamlet of Little Hautbois on the day I visit. The pub, once popular with airmen from RAF Coltishall, stopped being a pub a long time ago, even before RAF Coltishall stopped being RAF Coltishall. It’s not Saturday, so there are no weddings at Hautbois Hall. Nor is it 19 May, so the restless, headless ghost of Thomas Boleyn isn’t driving his carriage across the bridge over the River Bure, as he is said to do on the anniversary of the execution of his daughter, Anne. Today, a lovely autumn one, all is as it should be. But half a mile down a narrow country lane is an incongruous and baffling sight: a strip of gentle hillside made up of large white rectangular blocks, piled up and sparkling in the sunshine. A glacier, you might think, if you were in Norway rather than Norfolk.

items.title: China sees surge in border crossings amid visa-free travel boom
items.summary: China recorded a surge in border crossings by both mainland Chinese citizens and foreign nationals in the third quarter of this year, as Chinese companies expand overseas and Beijing steps up incentives to attract foreign tourists. The country logged a total of 192 million…
items.body: China recorded a surge in border crossings by both mainland Chinese citizens and foreign nationals in the third quarter of this year, as Chinese companies expand overseas and Beijing steps up incentives to attract foreign tourists. The country logged a total of 192 million border crossings in the July-September period, up 7.9 per cent year on year, according to data released by the National Immigration Administration on Tuesday. China received 11.6 million foreign arrivals, up 15.6 per cent, with visa-free entries surging 24.1 per cent to account for 77.5 per cent of the total. The top three sources of foreign visitors were Russia, South Korea and Vietnam in that order, followed by Malaysia, the United States, Japan, Singapore, Thailand and Australia, according to the data.

items.title: Netflix has dipped its toe into theatrical. Is it ready to jump in?
items.summary: Co-CEO Ted Sarandos has said the streamer needs new avenues for growth and to improve execution around its content strategy.
items.body: During the company's third-quarter earnings call on Tuesday, co-CEO Ted Sarandos reiterated the streaming giant's long-held stance that its content, which it spent $20 billion on last year, is meant for its subscribers and, therefore, should be delivered to customers on its streaming platform as quickly as possible. Yet, the company is set to have 30 theatrical releases in 2027, on par with what it brought to cinemas in 2026. And while not all of these features are expected to have wide releases or long runs in theaters, Netflix is testing the waters with projects like Greta Gerwig's "Narnia: The Magician's Nephew," which will have a wide release and a 49-day exclusive theatrical window when it hits cinemas in February. The company seems poised to carve a new path forward as it grapples with viewership stagnation and a stock slump of roughly 30% since January.

items.title: Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy
items.summary: Government decision is about how much oil and gas is sensible for UK to produce on the way to net zero Business live – latest updates Andy Burnham hit the nail on the (well)head in his first fortnight as prime minister when he said : “The question isn’t whether Britain will…
items.body: A ndy Burnham hit the nail on the (well)head in his first fortnight as prime minister when he said : “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is, where does it come from?” It was a nod towards several awkward energy facts. First, oil and gas provided 75% of the UK’s energy in 2025, government data shows. Second, even with the rollout of domestic renewables for generating electricity, about 43% of overall energy was imported last year. Third, all credible paths to net zero emissions by 2050 involve using a lot of oil and gas on the way because we’re still in the foothills of electrification. Fewer than 2% of UK households have heat pumps, according to the lobby group Electrify Britain. While sales of EVs are accelerating, nearly 95% of vehicles on the road run on petrol and diesel.

items.title: China’s youth unemployment rate edges down slightly but jobseekers still doing it tough
items.summary: China’s youth unemployment rate edged down slightly in September as some graduates secured jobs, but young jobseekers still face a tough market as employers increasingly look beyond academic qualifications for candidates with relevant work experience. The unemployment rate among…
items.body: China’s youth unemployment rate edged down slightly in September as some graduates secured jobs, but young jobseekers still face a tough market as employers increasingly look beyond academic qualifications for candidates with relevant work experience. The unemployment rate among people aged 16 to 24, excluding students, fell to 18 per cent in September from 18.9 per cent in August, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday. With around 12.7 million university graduates having entered the job market this year, a record high, the youth unemployment rate in August matched its level a year earlier, equalling its highest point since Beijing revised its calculation methodology in 2023 to exclude students. Weighed down by weak domestic demand and fierce competition, China’s job market remained sluggish last month.

The layoffs will affect approximately 1,000 employees. "As we work to capture the significant opportunity ahead, this step was taken to ensure we continue to operate from a position of strength by aligning our teams and resources with our top strategic priorities," the spokesperson said in a statement. The company also said it will continue to hire in "priority areas aligned with our strategy." As of the end of 2025, eBay had roughly 12,300 employees.

items.title: What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?
items.summary: Decision has implications for household energy bills, the UK economy and the climate crisis UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea Nils Pratley: Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy About four years and six energy secretaries after it was given the…
items.body: About four years and six energy secretaries after it was given the green light, the Jackdaw gasfield has been given consent to begin production 150 miles east of Aberdeen. So what does this long-awaited decision mean for the Labour party, household bills, the economy and the climate crisis? No, because although the party vowed to “not issue new licences to explore new fields” in the hydrocarbon-rich basin, it made clear it would honour licences granted before it came to power. These fields include Jackdaw, which was granted a licence in 2022 , and the larger Rosebank oilfield west of Shetland, which was approved the following year . Oil and gas licences give broad permission to explore an area for fossil fuels but consent is still needed to extract them.

items.body: China Cosco Shipping Holdings, the country’s largest ocean carrier, has prioritised resilience as it rolls out an emergency response system to cope with rising geopolitical conflicts, infrastructure bottlenecks and climate-related disruptions. The company is launching fresh capacity and new trade routes as part of the plan, as it looks to ensure its supply chains can withstand a mix of potential shocks, according to chairman Wan Min. “We believe that true resilience is not merely restricted to a single route,” he said at the North Bund Summit, a shipping industry ­conference, in Shanghai on Tuesday. “A fully resilient shipping system should comprise adequate backup to ensure a safe and stable operation through the entire supply chain.” Cosco had also added road transport into its routes as a way of dodging the impact of conflicts in the Middle East, the chairman added.

items.title: The Guardian view on drilling in Jackdaw: a truly pragmatic approach would focus on Britain’s green transition | Editorial
items.summary: Opening the North Sea gasfield will deliver minimal benefits for households, while sending a dismal signal before next month’s Cop summit This week a report from the UN Environment Programme concluded that holding global temperatures to a 1.5C warming limit – the centrepiece…
items.body: T his week a report from the UN Environment Programme concluded that holding global temperatures to a 1.5C warming limit – the centrepiece commitment of the Paris climate agreement – is no longer achievable. If the disastrous consequences of a significant overshoot are to be mitigated, it argued, governments must start delivering the short-term actions to meet long-term targets on reducing fossil fuel consumption. Disappointingly, Andy Burnham and his energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, took a different view of short-term priorities on Wednesday. Before the November Cop summit, where regaining lost momentum on climate action will be crucial, their decision to approve new drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield sent a dismal signal. The prime minister justified it as a pragmatic move “at a time when people are really struggling”. But the pragmatic arguments don’t stack up.

items.body: China plans to expand venture capital and long-term funding for technology companies in the Greater Bay Area while strengthening financial links between Hong Kong and the mainland, as part of efforts to turn the region into a leading innovation hub alongside Beijing and Shanghai. In guidelines published on Monday, the People’s Bank of China and 10 other government departments set out plans for “an open technology finance system” across the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area. The proposals included closer coordination of financial rules and fewer barriers to the cross-border movement of capital and other resources, while the broader aim is to improve financial services for technological innovation in three major economic regions: the Greater Bay Area and the areas surrounding Beijing and Shanghai.

items.body: New Mexico 's attorney general on Wednesday filed a federal lawsuit accusing Jeffrey Epstein 's long-time personal lawyer and accountant of facilitating Epstein's sex trafficking operation. The civil suit alleges the attorney, Darren Indyke, and the accountant, Richard Kahn, helped finance and conceal Epstein's sex trafficking, which included the abuse of girls and young women at his Zorro Ranch in Santa Fe County, New Mexico. Indyke and Kahn are beneficiaries of Epstein's 1953 Trust, co-executors of Epstein's estate, and administrators of the revocable trust, whose name comes from the year of the convicted sex offender's birth. New Mexico's suit asks a judge to block Indyke and Kahn from receiving payments from the estate as the case proceeds in U.S. District Court in New Mexico.

items.title: As Miatta ignites the speaker’s gas-fuelled inferno, Reform show up as snowflakes | John Crace
items.summary: The energy secretary’s trip north provokes Hoyle’s futile rage, while ITV’s Reform exposé leaves Zia Yusuf immensely sad When is a licence not a licence? When it’s a new licence that is an old licence. After months of faffing around – there were the small matters of a party…
items.body: W hen is a licence not a licence? When it’s a new licence that is an old licence. After months of faffing around – there were the small matters of a party conference and a byelection to negotiate first – the government finally gave the go-ahead to drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. What swung it wasn’t so much the irresistible excitement of creating 27 new jobs and securing 2% of the UK’s gas supply for the next 10 years, it was the politics. If other countries were going to carry on drilling then we might as well do so, too. There would still be the same amount of greenhouse gases created and we wouldn’t have to rely on anyone else for our gas supply. Though we would for the other 98%. Small steps and all that. At a time of global insecurity and rising energy costs, it was time to drill, baby, drill.

items.title: OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring — and one lied about it
items.summary: Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue AI models.
items.body: OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with one subsequently denying it had done so. An agent powered by GPT Sol 6.1 disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team, the company said in a blog post late on Tuesday. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration and then falsely claimed it hadn't. The incidents happened during internal coding tasks. "In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them," OpenAI said in a blog post.

items.title: Burnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a pen | Zoe Williams
items.summary: This foolish decision undermines hopes that this government will take the necessary steps the climate crisis demands When the news broke that the UK government had approved the Jackdaw gasfield , I was at a Guardian climate event at the Royal Geographical Society. Appropriately,…
items.body: W hen the news broke that the UK government had approved the Jackdaw gasfield , I was at a Guardian climate event at the Royal Geographical Society. Appropriately, the theme suggested by readers was what can the public actually do in the face of what feels like paralysing climate doom? There is so much going on that is hopeful: biodiversity tracking, river protection, rewilding. Shruti Suresh, from the independent watchdog Global Witness, told those in attendance that if they wanted to effect change, they should protest against Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project. The message was so well understood that it didn’t need labouring. The mood in the room when the news came in was one of audible dismay. People had just watched the minister for climate transition declare that she could see the challenges ahead and was ready for them.

items.title: Expanding AI trade is turning safety stocks into a 'Texas hedge'
items.summary: The growing AI trade is infiltrating traditionally safe sectors like utilities, making hedging more difficult.
items.body: When a hurricane looms, panic buying clears store shelves of household essentials like water, canned food, dry goods, and toilet paper. A similar dynamic is playing out in the market. Investors are bailing on higher-volatility growth stocks and running toward the shelter of perceived safety sectors like utilities and consumer staples. The key difference? They may not be so safe. As valuation multiples across capital-intensive AI infrastructure plays — such as specialized data center hosting providers CoreWeave (CRWV) and Iren Ltd (IREN) — take on water in the form of massive debt loads due to aggressive capex buildouts, investors may want to take a portion of their equity exposure into more protected water.

items.title: A plan to ensure energy is affordable for all | Letters
items.summary: Dr Alex Chapman calls for a government-funded price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas, in response to an article by Nils Pratley Nils Pratley thinks that the secretary of state, Miatta Fahnbulleh, should “keep things simple” and develop a targeted social tariff to…
items.body: Nils Pratley thinks that the secretary of state, Miatta Fahnbulleh, should “keep things simple” and develop a targeted social tariff to protect vulnerable households from surging energy bills ( The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff, 14 October ). Unfortunately, there is nothing simple about such a scheme. Pratley’s proposal would mean creating a new benefits system inside our privatised energy industry. If the interminable debates about our current benefits system were not enough to put him off, we can look to the failing social care system to see where it might lead. Andy Burnham has made it his life’s mission to dismantle this lottery that can strip pensioners of their savings and the family home. Just as he now plans a universal public provision of adult social care, we at the New Economics Foundation have such a plan for energy.

In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way illegal working fines are issued and collected.

items.title: U.S. eyes refining muscle of Indian billionaire Ambani's Reliance as Rubio visits Jamnagar plant
items.summary: Rubio said the "extraordinary" refining capacity of Reliance could help India diversify its energy supplies, hinting at greater offtake of Venezuelan crude.
items.body: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will discuss refining Western energy supplies with Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries when he visits the company's plant in Jamnagar, Gujarat — the world's largest single-site refinery. The U.S. is looking to "work together more closely" with Reliance for refining energy from the "Western Hemisphere," Rubio said in an interview with India's Network 18, which is owned by Reliance. "I think that's helpful to India, but it's also helpful to us," he added. Reliance's Jamnagar refinery, which Rubio will visit on Wednesday, has a crude processing capacity of 1.4 million barrels per day. Reliance has also emerged as the biggest buyer of Venezuelan crude outside of the U.S., as of end-September.

items.title: ‘I can charge my car for £6’: could new rules cut costs for EV drivers?
items.summary: Owners in England with no driveway can now slash their costs by installing a cross-pavement gully – but it’s a postcode lottery When Alison Williams bought her electric Volkswagen ID.3 two years ago, she thought she was making the right choice for the environment, having already…
items.body: W hen Alison Williams bought her electric Volkswagen ID.3 two years ago, she thought she was making the right choice for the environment, having already upgraded her end-of-terrace London home with insulation and solar panels. However, charging the car has proved more costly than she hoped, as she is not able to install the cross-pavement gully – a narrow electric vehicle cable channel embedded in the pavement – that she would need to charge at home. That will remain the case despite a change in the law. From Wednesday, drivers in England who do not have off-street parking will no longer need to get planning permission to put in a pavement gully outside their home. The gullies sit flush within the pavement and allow an EV charging cable to reach a parked vehicle without creating a trip hazard.

items.title: Oil prices mixed as traders assess Middle East developments
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Tuesday that naval mines had prevented three tankers attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
items.body: Oil prices were mixed Wednesday as worries over Middle East supply disruptions keep the market on edge, with attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy facilities denting sentiment. Brent crude futures added 3 cents to close at $108.82 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude fell 67 cents to settle at $97.15 a barrel. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Tuesday that naval mines had prevented three tankers attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz using routes Tehran deemed unauthorized. "Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," IRGC said in a statement published on their official Sepah News website .

items.title: Cybersecurity companies urge Indonesia to boost AI talent
items.body: BALI, Indonesia -- Cybersecurity-related companies in Indonesia say the nation must rapidly expand the number of AI experts in its workforce to protect Southeast Asia's largest economy from cyberattacks and online scams, as well as urging the government to improve support for the artificial intelligence sector.

items.title: UK cinemas report ‘bonkers’ demand for documentary You Can See Everything
items.summary: Tickets for film about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes said to be selling out after $15m opening weekend in the US It is the film everyone seems to be talking about, spawning memes and fuelling feverish online debate about its subject, the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth…
items.body: It is the film everyone seems to be talking about, spawning memes and fuelling feverish online debate about its subject, the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Now, a month before Nathan Fielder’s documentary You Can See Everything reaches UK cinemas, tickets for screenings are already selling out after its remarkable $15m (£11.3m) opening weekend in the US. Clare Binns, the creative director of Picturehouse Cinemas, said the excitement was reminiscent of the response to Greta Gerwig’s Barbie, which became a global box-office phenomenon in 2023. “People are hungry in a way that we haven’t really seen since then,” she said.

items.title: Treasury yields steady as investors await jobless claims
items.summary: Treasury yields steadied as investors await more data for insights into the U.S. economic picture.
items.body: Treasury yields steadied on Wednesday as investors awaited fresh data for insights into the U.S. economic picture ahead of next week's Federal Reserve interest rate decision. The yield on 10-year U.S. Treasury — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was up less than 1 basis point at 5.123%. The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, rose more than 2 basis points to 4.808%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasurys — which often moves on geopolitical developments — moved more than 1 basis point lower to 5.411%. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another. With the Federal Reserve's next interest rate meeting scheduled for Oct.
